stimulus.text: Two engravings from Theodor de Bry's America series (1591), after drawings by Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues. The first shows Florida Indians planting seeds of beans and maize in cleared fields. The second shows the same people hunting deer disguised under deerskins. De Bry never visited North America; he engraved the scenes in Europe from watercolors painted by Jacques Le Moyne, a French artist with the Laudonnière expedition.
stimulus.source_note: Engravings from the shared image pool; Theodor de Bry (1591), after Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues, public domain (Library of Congress).

stem: The first engraving shows the same people planting beans and maize. The second shows them hunting deer disguised under deerskins. What do the two engravings together best demonstrate?

options.text: Hunting mattered far more than farming to every Native society in the Americas.
options.misconception: Reads one region's hunting as proof about every society in the Americas.

options.text: Native peoples combined farming with hunting instead of relying on one food source.
Native peoples gave up farming entirely once they learned to hunt deer.
options.misconception: Turns two practices side by side into one replacing the other.

options.text: Only societies with no farming at all ever hunted animals for food.
options.misconception: Claims farming peoples never hunted, but this example shows they did.

rationales.A: The engravings show one region's people doing both jobs, which cannot prove anything about every society in the Americas.
rationales.B: The same community is shown both planting crops and hunting deer, so its economy mixed farming with hunting.
rationales.C: The two engravings show both practices existing side by side, not one replacing the other.
rationales.D: This very example shows a farming people hunting too, so farming and hunting were not separate worlds.
rationales.general:
1. Watch the first scene. People plant beans and maize in cleared fields, the work of farmers.
2. Watch the second. The same people hunt deer, disguised under deerskins, the work of hunters.
3. Put the two jobs in one household. One community farms and hunts, so its food comes from two sources at once.
4. Reject either half alone. Farming alone misses the hunt, and hunting alone misses the fields.
Remember: when two images show the same people doing different work, read them as one mixed economy.
